refnamediv.refpurpose: Information about rotation of GPG keys and subkeys for flatpak repositories

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: Flatpak encourages the commits and summary metadata for a repository to be cryptographically signed with a GPG key which is known to all clients using the repository. This allows the clients to verify the authenticity and integrity of data from the repository.

Since flatpak 1.20, it additionally supports an out-of-band key update mechanism, to allow the repository to publish updates to its signing key in a way which can be picked up by clients. This is needed to allow key rotation, for example. Prior to flatpak 1.20 this would only have been possible by manually updating the key in the repository configuration of each client.

This out-of-band key update mechanism has two parts: a standard GPG keyring served over HTTP, which contains the latest copy of the public keys from the repository’s signing keyring; and a xa.gpg-keys-url entry in the repository’s summary file, which points to it. Clients download and cache a copy of the keyring and, whenever it has changed, verify and import keys from it into their local keyring (repo/${remote}.trustedkeys.gpg), which is then used to verify repository signatures as normal.

refsect1.title: Security Model
refsect1.para: The out-of-band update mechanism is only used on repositories which have GPG signing (and GPG signed summary files) enabled. This gives authenticity and integrity guarantees on the URI stored in the xa.gpg-keys-url summary entry.

It is recommended that the xa.gpg-keys-url is a HTTPS URI, which gives authenticity and integrity guarantees on its downloaded content (assuming its origin is under the control of the repository owner).

Keys are conditionally imported from the downloaded keyring into the local keyring which forms the trust root for verification of repository signatures. When importing, the current contents of the local keyring form the initial trust root. During the import, the trust root grows as new keys pass validation; this allows for signature chains between new keys.
New subkeys of keys in the trust root are always imported, as by construction they are already signed by a key in the trust root (their primary key).
Each new primary key is imported if all the following conditions are met:

listitem.para: It is not revoked, disabled or invalid.
It contains at least one UID which is not revoked or invalid.
That UID is signed by a key already in the trust root, and that signature is more recent than any revoked signatures, and is not expired or invalid.
The import limit (of 20 new keys) has not been reached.

refsect1.para: New revocation certificates and revocation signatures are always imported if they pertain to a key in the trust root.

New primary keys which have expired are imported (if they meet all the other criteria), as they may have been used to sign other new primary keys before expiry. They will be marked as expired in the local keyring after import. This can happen in situations where a client has not updated from the repository across multiple key rotations, so their current local trust root only contains keys which are great-ancestors of the current signing key. The model here can be thought of as GPG forbidding new signatures to be created with an expired key, but continuing to allow verification of signatures using that key (unless it has been revoked).

GPG has various web-of-trust and trust-on-first-use (TOFU) features for determining whether to trust a key. Because each flatpak repository is a trusted centralised point for key distribution, these features are not needed and are not used in the import process. These features include the local trust database (trustdb.gpg) and ‘ownertrust’.

The downloaded keyring is assumed to be non-malicious to the extent that this is required by GPG’s code which handles loading an unknown external keyring. Risks from injected malicious (malformed) keyrings can be mitigated by providing a HTTPS xa.gpg-keys-url, rather than a HTTP one.

refsect1.title: System Administration
refsect1.para: The out-of-band update mechanism has been designed for the main purpose of allowing key rotation. A typical GPG key setup for a secure flatpak repository is to have a master key KM (stored offline and airgapped), and a signing subkey KS1 (stored in a hardware security module on the server which builds commits and pushes them to the repository). KM has no expiry date and is closely guarded. KS1 has an expiry date on the order of months to years, to reduce the fallout if its private key were to become public. At the time of generating KS1, it is signed by KM (which makes it a subkey). The public key material for both keys is published as the repository’s keyring, and configured in the local keyring of all clients when they add the remote.

Before KS1 expires, a new signing subkey KS2 must be generated, signed by KM, its private key put onto a hardware security module on the server, and its public key distributed to all clients which use the repository. Equivalently, the metadata of KS1 could be updated to extend its expiry date if there is confidence that it has not been compromised. The former approach is more conventional as it eliminates the risk of KS1 having been compromised. Both approaches equivalently require the distribution of new public key material to clients.

Another possible approach is to generate a new master key K'M, a new signing subkey K'S1, and then sign K'M with KM. This approach might be preferred to allow changing key parameters (such as algorithm or key size) if needed. It is equivalent to both approaches above in as much as it also requires the distribution of new public key material to clients.
From a system administration point of view, this process requires several steps:

listitem.para: Months in advance of the key expiry date, generate the new signing subkey KS2 on the server’s hardware security module, alongside the existing KS1. Sign it with KM, ensuring that KM stays offline and airgapped. For example (on an airgapped machine):

para.programlisting: # Copy the master key (including private key) into $TEMP_HOMEDIR, then gpg --homedir "${TEMP_HOMEDIR}" --edit-key "${KM_FINGERPRINT}" addkey change-usage expire cross-certify save # Use hardware security module specific commands to copy the new KS2 onto the # server’s HSM, then # Copy the updated "${TEMP_HOMEDIR}" to its airgapped offline storage location # for future use, then shred --remove "${TEMP_HOMEDIR}"

listitem.para: Export the public keyring for the server, containing the public keys of KM, KS1 and KS2. Publish this .gpg file over HTTPS on the flatpak repository server, and configure aggressive caching for it. HTTP ETag support plus a max-age on the order of weeks or months is recommended, as the cache policy set by the server will affect how often every client using the repository downloads the keyring. For example:

para.programlisting: gpg --homedir "${HOMEDIR}" --output "www/repos/${REPO}.published.gpg" --armor --export "${KM_FINGERPRINT}" "${KS1_FINGERPRINT}" "${KS2_FINGERPRINT}" # Add appropriate server-specific caching configuration

Note the trailing ! on the fingerprints. This is required to force GPG to use the given subkey, instead of potentially choosing a different signing subkey from the same primary key.
Set the xa.gpg-keys-url entry in the repository’s summary file to point to the newly published keyring. For example:

After KS1 expires, it can be removed from the server’s hardware security module and commits and the summary file no longer need to be signed with it; only with KS2 from now on. Key rotation is complete.
